decisions.decision: How should classifications be computed and delivered?
decisions.context: The classifier processes millions of documents daily, and the brief gives no interactive latency requirement. Results must be consumed by several teams.

alternatives.label: Scheduled batch prediction deployment
pros: Volume: scores large workloads on a schedule
Teams: writes results to shared storage
cons: Freshness: results wait for the next run

alternatives.label: Queue-fronted online serving cluster
cons: Cost: keeps online serving capacity available

decisions.rationale: The daily volume and lack of a stated latency target favor batch scoring; the sources “Architecting a Machine Learning Pipeline” and “Three Levels of ML Software” describe scheduled batch deployment. This gives up immediate results, which the brief does not require.
consequences: Teams consume persisted results after each scoring run.
Define the scoring schedule and freshness expectations.

decisions.decision: How should compute capacity handle seasonal variation?
decisions.context: Workload varies strongly over the year, so fixed capacity risks either peak overload or unused capacity outside peak periods.

alternatives.label: Elastic resource scaling
pros: Volume: scales for large processing demand
cons: Operations: requires scaling rules and monitoring

alternatives.label: Scale-to-zero serving
cons: Volume: may need capacity startup during peaks

decisions.rationale: Seasonal volume and daily scale make elastic resource scaling the stronger fit; “Architecting a Machine Learning Pipeline” and “Productionizing Machine Learning with a Microservices Architecture” describe scaling with workload. This favors peak capacity over eliminating all idle serving cost.
consequences: Capacity must be monitored against workload and scaling limits.
Some capacity may remain allocated between peaks.

decisions.decision: How should consuming teams access classifications?
decisions.context: Several teams consume the classifier’s results, so the system needs a shared integration boundary. The brief does not specify synchronous access or latency targets.

alternatives.label: REST prediction microservice
pros: Teams: shared API boundary for integrations
Volume: separates classifier service from consumers
cons: Operations: adds a service to maintain

decisions.rationale: A shared REST interface suits several independently consuming teams; “How to power up your product by machine learning with python microservice” and “Architecting a Machine Learning Pipeline” describe API-backed prediction services. This adds service operations overhead compared with distributing a model representation.
consequences: Define and version a stable request and response contract.
The brief does not specify whether consumers call synchronously or read batch results.

decisions.decision: How should production quality drift be detected?
decisions.context: Operators need to see when classification quality drifts. The design space’s monitoring dimension has low exclusivity, so quality and input-drift monitoring can be combined.

alternatives.label: Input and feature-drift monitoring
pros: Drift visibility: detects changing inputs and features
cons: Quality: input shifts do not prove accuracy loss

alternatives.label: Real-time prediction-quality monitoring
pros: Quality: measures model behavior when labels arrive
cons: Volume: depends on collecting and evaluating labels

alternatives.label: Software-metrics-only monitoring
pros: Volume: tracks operational metrics at scale

decisions.rationale: The brief explicitly needs visibility into quality drift, so combine input and feature-drift monitoring with prediction-quality measurement when labels become available. “MLOps: Continuous delivery and automation pipelines in machine learning” and “Machine Learning Monitoring: What It Is, and What We Are Missing” support these practices; this costs additional effort to collect labels and evaluate quality.
consequences: Track input and feature distributions alongside quality metrics.
Quality measurement depends on labeled outcomes becoming available.
Set alert thresholds and ownership for investigation.

uncovered: How labels are produced and how often they become available.
Whether and when detected drift should trigger retraining or human review.
Required latency, freshness, availability, and seasonal peak capacity targets.
Classification result retention, access control, and privacy requirements.
The schema, delivery mechanism, and ownership expectations for each consuming team.
